p111: 111.  As regards more specifically the reasoning of the Latvian courts, the Court observes that at first instance the court dismissed, with reasons, the applicant’s objections to the child’s return under Article 13 of the Hague Convention, in particular after examining the documents produced by the parties, namely photographs and copies of e-mails exchanged between the applicant and T.’s relatives, and witness statements produced by the applicant. However, after refusing to ask the Australian authorities for information about T.’s previous convictions and the charges allegedly brought against him, the court ultimately dismissed the allegation of a risk of psychological harm to the child in the event of her immediate separation from her mother, on the ground that the applicant had failed to substantiate it (see paragraph 21 above).
p112: 112.  The Court notes that the situation subsequently presented itself differently before the Rīga Regional Court, as the applicant had produced, in the context of her appeal, a certificate drawn up at her request by a psychologist on 16 December 2008, that is, after the first-instance judgment. That document indicated that, although the child’s young age prevented her from expressing a preference as to her place of residence, an immediate separation from her mother was to be ruled out on account of the risk of psychological trauma (see paragraph 22 above).
p113: 113.  While the District Court, when examining the application for a stay of execution of the judgment ordering the child’s return, took that factor into account in ordering, in the child’s interests, a stay of execution of the return order pending the examination of the appeal (see paragraph 24 above), the Regional Court, for its part, rejected it.
p114: 114.  The Court notes that the appellate judges considered that the conclusion of the psychological examination concerned the merits of the custody issue and could not therefore serve as evidence in deciding the issue of return before them. In so doing, on the basis of that reasoning, the Rīga Regional Court refused to examine the conclusions of that expert report in the light of the provisions of Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention, even though it was directly related to the best interests of the child, since it referred to a risk of psychological trauma for the child in the event of her immediate separation from her mother (contrast Maumousseau and Washington, cited above, § 63).
p115: 115.  Article 8 of the Convention imposed a procedural obligation on the Latvian authorities, requiring an arguable allegation of “grave risk” to the child in the event of return to be effectively examined by the courts and their findings to be set out in a reasoned decision (see paragraph 107 above).
p116: 116.  Under Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention, the courts examining a return request are not bound to grant it if “the person, institution or other body which opposes its return establishes that ... there is a grave risk”. It is first for the parent who opposes the return to adduce sufficient evidence to this effect. In the present case, it was therefore for the applicant to provide sufficient evidence to substantiate her allegations, which, moreover, had to concern the existence of a risk which was specifically described by Article 13 (b) as “grave”. The Court notes, furthermore, that while Article 13 (b) is not restrictive as to the exact nature of the “grave risk” – which could entail not only “physical or psychological harm” but also “an intolerable situation” –, it cannot be read, in the light of Article 8 of the Convention, as including all of the inconveniences necessarily linked to the experience of return: the exception provided for in Article 13 (b) concerns only situations which go beyond what a child might reasonably bear. The applicant complied with that obligation by producing a certificate drawn up by a psychologist, concluding that there was a risk of trauma for the child in the event of her immediate separation from her mother. She also submitted that T. had criminal convictions and referred to instances of ill-treatment on his part. It was therefore for the Latvian courts to carry out meaningful checks enabling them either to confirm or to exclude the existence of a “grave risk” (see B. v. Belgium, no. 4320/11, §§ 70-72, 10 July 2012).
